summary.text: A 32-year-old Iranian Caucasian woman, gravida 3 para 2 with a history of one IUFD and one neonatal death, was referred in July 2023 for elevated serum bile acid levels and was diagnosed with recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. She had no history of consanguineous marriage or family history of liver or autoimmune disorders and a normal BMI of 22.5.

In her first pregnancy she developed gestational hypertension without proteinuria at 28 weeks, generalized pruritus and mildly elevated liver enzymes with an unremarkable liver ultrasound. Bile acid testing was unavailable, so UDCA was empirically started for suspected ICP. An emergency cesarean section at 29 weeks for fetal distress and worsening hypertension was followed by neonatal death within 24 hr, postpartum magnesium sulfate and oral antihypertensives, negative hepatitis serologies and liver enzymes that remained elevated three months postpartum.

In her second pregnancy mild pruritus recurred, UDCA was restarted, liver enzymes were moderately elevated and bile acid testing remained unavailable. IUFD was confirmed at 24 weeks and a 600-gr male fetus was delivered vaginally, with placental histopathology showing massive chronic histiocytic intervillositis. Antiphospholipid tests were negative; after gastroenterology consultation UDCA, hydroxychloroquine and prednisolone were started for suspected autoimmune-related liver dysfunction, and autoimmune hepatitis was ruled out.

The third, planned pregnancy was managed with enoxaparin, aspirin, prednisolone, hydroxychloroquine and UDCA. Bile acid levels were elevated, an anomaly scan showed echogenic bowel loops, aneuploidy screening was low-risk and weekly assessments were normal. UDCA and prednisolone doses were increased, gestational diabetes was diagnosed at 28 weeks and treated with insulin, and she was admitted at 32 weeks with worsening pruritus. Bile acid peaked at 333 μmol/L despite treatment, a multidisciplinary decision to deliver was made, and a 1980-gr male infant was delivered by cesarean section at 32 weeks.

The neonate needed nasal CPAP and NICU admission for low oxygen saturation, had elevated C-reactive protein and a Klebsiella-positive blood culture treated with amikacin and cefoxitin then meropenem and vancomycin, and received phototherapy for hyperbilirubinemia. Failure to pass meconium led to imaging suggestive of Hirschsprung disease, then exploratory surgery with ileostomy; biopsies excluded the diagnosis. The infant received parenteral nutrition and red cell transfusion and was discharged three weeks post-surgery, with neonatal recovery and maternal symptom resolution postpartum.
